text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic has pledged to investigate opposition protests against vote rigging but has rejected international criticism of the electoral crisis gripping Serbia.

Milosevic had his first meeting with students in month-old demonstrations against annulled local election results on Tuesday as another massive rally took place in Belgrade and more protests were held in 36 other towns.

Washington has led Western attacks on effective one-party rule in Serbia demanding that Milosevic, who has remained aloof in the affair, accept defeat in Belgrade and other towns in local elections held on November 17.

A delegation of students who had marched from the southern industrial city of Nis, where a court on Sunday ordered an electoral commission to recognise an opposition victory there, handed a protest letter and spoilt ballot papers to Milosevic.

"Neither you nor I count votes, but I shall ask the government to instruct the justice ministry to very carefully study all the facts contained in the documents which you have given me," Milosevic told the students.

At the meeting, later broadcast on state-run television which has carried scant footage of the protests, he said: "Mistakes are always possible...I assure you that this state will not protect anyone who has broken the law, be they citizens or officials."
The president added: "We must also make it very clear that regardless of any visits your leaders make to embassies or foreign capitals, a foreign hand will never govern Serbia."

Milosevic met leading officials of his Socialist party on Tuesday night to discuss strategy as the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition vowed to once again flood the streets of Serbia's cities and towns on Wednesday in daily demonstrations.
There were more than 100,000 opposition supporters at Tuesday's march in central Belgrade. Socialist mayor Nebojsa Covic was jeered when he appeared on a balcony at city hall.
Courts in Nis and Smederevska Palanka have ordered the socialists to turn control of both towns over to Zajedno in an endorsement of the fraud claims.
In a sign that Milosevic might give way in Belgrade, the main prize for the opposition, Zajedno said the Serbian supreme court had upheld its victory in the Savski Venac municipality.

The independent Belgrade FoNet news agency said an opinion poll conducted in the capital showed 58 percent of 500 people questioned were optimistic that Zajedno would win its struggle. Just 13 percent feared the unrest risked sliding into violence after the West threatened Milosevic with reprisals if he unleashed his police against peaceful demonstrators.

The president has invited the Organisation for Cooperation and Security in Europe (OSCE) to send a team to verify the results. OSCE said in a letter to Zajedno on Tuesday the team, headed by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, would arrive before Christmas.
